questions.q: Per this lesson, which direction does data flow in a graphical execution plan?
options: Right-to-left and bottom-to-top — the rightmost, bottom-most operators (typically table/index access) run first
Left-to-right, the same way English text reads
Top-to-bottom only, direction left-right is irrelevant
The direction is random and depends on the query
questions.explain: Base table or index access operators sit at the right/bottom and run first; data flows left and up until it reaches the SELECT operator, the final result.

questions.q: What does a Key Lookup operator represent?
options: A secondary trip back to the clustered index to fetch columns not included in the nonclustered index used for the seek, happening once per matching row
A full scan of every row in a table
The operator that always runs first in any plan
A join type used only for very large tables
questions.explain: A Key Lookup fetches additional columns from the clustered index for each row a nonclustered index seek matched — cheap individually, expensive at scale.

questions.q: What does the thickness of the arrows (data flow lines) between operators actually represent?
options: The number of rows flowing through that point in the plan — not cost and not time
The exact CPU cost of that operator
The number of logical reads at that step
How long, in seconds, that step of the plan took to execute
questions.explain: Arrow thickness is proportional to row count. A thick arrow persisting where you expected filtering can be a visual clue that a predicate isn't being applied as expected.

questions.q: How should the operator cost percentage shown in a plan be interpreted, per this lesson?
options: As the optimizer's estimated relative cost within that one specific plan — a good lead for investigation, but not proof, and it can be wrong
As an exact, measured real-world cost in milliseconds
As directly comparable across two completely different queries
As a guarantee that the highest-percentage operator is always the true bottleneck
questions.explain: Cost percentages come from the optimizer's cost model at compile time; they can be misleading when statistics are stale or an estimate was otherwise wrong.

questions.q: What does an Index Seek operator indicate, versus an Index Scan?
options: A Seek means the engine navigated the index's B-tree directly to the needed rows (efficient); a Scan means it read every row in the index
They are functionally identical operators with different names
A Seek always costs more than a Scan
A Scan means the query used no index at all, ever
questions.explain: Seeks are targeted lookups via the B-tree; Scans read the whole structure, which is fine for small tables but a red flag on a large table for a selective query.
